Stachelbeere.et: Stachel + Beere (“berry”). The term has been attested since at least the late 16th century; the 1607 dictionary Dictionnaire François-Allemand & Allemand-François contains the variant forms "Stachelbeer" and "Stichelbeer".

s: Ein Kaktus hat keine Stacheln, sondern Dornen, während eine Rose keine Dornen, sondern Stacheln hat.
A cactus has no spines, only thorns, while a rose has prickles but no thorns.
Stachel.et: From Middle High German stachel, from Late Old High German stahhil, from Old High German stakulla, from an extension of stechen with nominalizing suffix -ila.

Stachelschwein.et: 16th century, from Stachel (“spine, spike”) + Schwein (“pig, swine”), a calque of Latin porcus spīnōsus, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros).

Stack.et: Borrowed from Low German Stack, from Middle Low German stak. Probably related with stāke (“stake”). Possibly influenced by stacket (“stockade, picket fence”), itself from also related Old French estakete.

s: prickly cucumber (Echinocystis lobata; a plant in the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) with spiny fruits)
Chayote, some varieties of which have spiny fruits.
Any mollusc of the proposed clade Aculifera.
synonym of Faschine (“fascine, bundle of sticks used for damming”)
synonym of Karlsplatz, a large square in central Munich, Bavaria.
Stachus.et: Alteration of Eustach, familiar form of Eustachius (compare English Eustace), the name of an 18th-century innkeeper who kept a beer garden on the square.
